tldr: Headlines across all 15 buckets frame Trump's White House media ban primarily as a legal confrontation — lawsuits, court hearings, and the 'access is a privilege' doctrine dominate globally. The press-pool solidarity boycott is the secondary headline angle, prominent in pan-African, Turkish, and wire-service coverage, while U.S. and Brussels-beltway outlets uniquely surface 'national security' as itself a newsworthy framing device.

single_outlet_findings.note: Only headline in the corpus to frame the ban as exposure of a pre-existing journalistic fraud ('The Biggest Scam In American Journalism EXPOSED') rather than a press-freedom crisis — the lone headline that treats the ban as justified rather than alarming.

Only headline to use 'national security' as the rhetorical subject itself, calling it Trump's 'executive sledgehammer' — foregrounds the pattern of invocation rather than the specific ban, diverging from every other outlet's event-centered framing.

Only headline to invert the power dynamic: 'Did Trump just silence himself?' frames the ban as potentially self-defeating rather than a successful exercise of executive control — a reflexive angle absent from all other titles.

Only headline to put direct speech front and centre: ''UN allowed us in, sir'' dramatizes a reporter confronting Trump, foregrounding individual defiance over the institutional legal battle that dominates every other outlet's title.

bottom_line: At the headline layer, global coverage collapses this story into a First Amendment court battle — lawsuits, court hearings, and the 'privilege not a right' doctrine span 11 of 15 buckets — while the solidarity boycott reads as a secondary signal exclusive to pan-African, Turkish, and wire-service titles, and the 'national security' framing appears only in U.S. and Brussels-beltway outlets.
